title: Newton's Method for Systems
short: Solve J(x) Δ = −F(x) with the Jacobian matrix J, then update x to x + Δ.
trouble: Students put the partial derivatives in the wrong places (row i holds the partials of Fᵢ), or forget the minus sign on F(x).

blocks.html: To solve several equations in several unknowns, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$, Newton's idea carries over: replace $\mathbf{F}$ by its linear approximation and solve that. The derivative becomes a matrix of Partial Derivatives, and dividing by it becomes solving a linear system, which you know from Inverses by Gauss–Jordan. Its convergence matches Newton's method in one variable.
For $\mathbf{F} = (F_1, \ldots, F_n)$, the Jacobian $J(\mathbf{x})$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with $$J_{ij} = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}:$$ row $i$ holds the partial derivatives of $F_i$.

Newton's method for systems: solve $$J(\mathbf{x}_k)\,\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k),$$ then set $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Delta}$. Near a root where $J$ is invertible it converges quadratically.

Linearize: $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Delta}) \approx \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k) + J(\mathbf{x}_k)\boldsymbol{\Delta}$. Setting the right side to $\mathbf{0}$ gives the linear system for the step. Writing $\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -J^{-1}\mathbf{F}$ shows the analogy with $-\frac{f}{f'}$, but in practice one solves the system by elimination; forming $J^{-1}$ costs more and is less accurate.

blocks.title: One step
steps: Solve $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Delta} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$: subtracting the equations gives $3\Delta_1 = 0$, so $\Delta_1 = 0$ and $\Delta_2 = -\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: Watching it converge
steps: The root is $x = \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{3}} \approx 1.931852$, $y = \frac{1}{x} \approx 0.517638$. Errors: about $7 \times 10^{-2}$, $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$, $1 \times 10^{-6}$: digits roughly doubling.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The circle x² + y² = 4 and the hyperbola xy = 1 meet in four points. Newton's method from (2, 1) heads for the one near (1.93, 0.52).

blocks.html: Each step costs more than in one variable. Building $J$ takes $n^{2}$ partial derivatives, and solving the linear system by elimination takes about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ operations (see The Cost of Elimination). For large systems, methods that update an approximate Jacobian instead of recomputing it (quasi-Newton methods) are common.

Plotting the curves first, as above, is a good way to choose a starting point. A system can have several roots; which one Newton's method finds depends on the start. Here the curves meet in four points, $(\pm 1.93, \pm 0.52)$ and $(\pm 0.52, \pm 1.93)$ with matching signs, and the start $(2, 1)$ leads to the nearest one. A sketch of the curves is the best way to choose starting guesses.

Putting the partial derivatives in the wrong places, or forgetting the minus sign. Row $i$ of $J$ holds $\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial y}, \ldots$; the system is $J\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -\mathbf{F}$. Check: if $\mathbf{F}$ were linear, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$, one Newton step from anywhere must land exactly on the solution.
